per_claim.claim: The speed of light in vacuum is exactly 299,792,458 metres per second.

judgments.passage_text: The speed of light in vacuum, commonly denoted c, is a universal physical constant equal to exactly 299,792,458 metres per second (approximately 300,000 km/s or 186,000 mi/s). According to the special theory of relativity, c is the upper limit for the speed at which conventional matter, energy, or any signal carrying information can travel through space. In 1983, the metre was redefined in the International System of Units (SI) as the distance travelled by light in vacuum in 1/299,792,458 of a second, making the speed of light in vacuum exact by definition.
judgments.evidence: The speed of light in vacuum, commonly denoted c, is a universal physical constant equal to exactly 299,792,458 metres per second
judgments.reason: L'evidenza afferma esattamente la stessa velocità della luce nel vuoto, con lo stesso valore numerico.

judgments.passage_text: The metre is the fundamental unit of length in the International System of Units (SI). Since 1983, the metre has been defined as the length of the path travelled by light in vacuum during a time interval of exactly 1/299,792,458 of a second. This definition fixes the speed of light to exactly 299,792,458 metres per second. Previously, the metre had been defined in terms of a physical artefact—a platinum-iridium bar kept at the International Bureau of Weights and Measures in Sèvres, France.
judgments.evidence: This definition fixes the speed of light to exactly 299,792,458 metres per second.
judgments.reason: L'evidenza afferma direttamente che la definizione fissa la velocità della luce a 299,792,458 metri al secondo, supportando esplicitamente il claim.

per_claim.claim: Ole Rømer was a Danish astronomer.

judgments.passage_text: Ole Christensen Rømer (25 September 1644 – 19 September 1710) was a Danish astronomer who made the first quantitative measurements of the speed of light. In 1676, Rømer observed that the periods of Jupiter's innermost moon, Io, appeared to be shorter when Earth was approaching Jupiter than when it was receding. He correctly attributed this difference to the varying time it takes light to travel from Jupiter to Earth. His estimate of the speed of light was approximately 220,000 km/s, which, although lower than the actual value, was a groundbreaking achievement in physics.

per_claim.claim: Hippolyte Fizeau measured the speed of light using a rotating toothed wheel in 1849.

judgments.passage_text: The Fizeau–Foucault apparatus is an instrument used to measure the speed of light. Hippolyte Fizeau first measured the terrestrial speed of light in 1849 using a rotating toothed wheel, obtaining a value of approximately 313,300 km/s. Léon Foucault improved on this in 1862 using a rotating mirror, obtaining 298,000 km/s—very close to the modern value. Albert Michelson later achieved extremely precise measurements using improved rotating mirror methods between 1877 and 1931.

Eiffel's company, Compagnie des Établissements Eiffel, was responsible for constructing many bridges and viaducts across France during the late 19th century. The Eiffel Tower was initially criticised by prominent French artists and intellectuals as an eyesore, but later became a globally recognised symbol of France.

per_claim.claim: Gustave Eiffel's company built the Eiffel Tower.

judgments.passage_text: The Eiffel Tower is a wrought-iron lattice tower on the Champ de Mars in Paris, France. It is named after the engineer Gustave Eiffel, whose company designed and built the tower from 1887 to 1889 as the entrance arch for the 1889 World's Fair. The tower is 330 metres (1,083 ft) tall, about the same height as an 81-storey building, and the tallest structure in Paris. Its base is square, measuring 125 metres (410 ft) on each side. During its construction, the Eiffel Tower surpassed the Washington Monument to become the tallest man-made structure in the world, a title it held for 41 years until the Chrysler Building in New York City was finished in 1930.
